RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care 
Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed 
Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges [CMS-0062-P] 
 
Dear Administrator Oz and National Coordinator Keane, 
 
On behalf of The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS), I write to provide comments on the Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule. Founded in 1964, STS is a not-for-profit 
organization representing more than 8,000 surgeons, researchers, and allied health care professionals 
worldwide who are dedicated to ensuring the best possible outcomes for surgeries of the heart, lungs, and 
esophagus, as well as other surgical procedures within the chest.  
 
Proposed Requirement to Incorporate Drugs Covered Under a Medical Benefit into the Prior  
Authorization API for All Impacted Payers 
 
CMS proposes to require impacted payers to enhance their Prior Authorization (PA) Application Programming 
Interfaces (APIs) by incorporating PA coverage and documentation requirements for drugs covered under a 
medical benefit, beginning October 1, 2027. 
 
 
 
 
 
STS applauds CMS's efforts to enhance PA APIs to include coverage and documentation requirements for drugs 
covered under the medical benefit. Improving the accessibility and transparency of PA requirements has the 
potential to reduce administrative burden and mitigate delays in patient access to necessary therapies. 
 
Delays associated with PA for drugs and related services are well documented and can significantly impede 
timely patient care. National survey data indicate that nearly 90% of physicians report PA delays access to 
necessary treatment, with many linking these delays to worsening clinical outcomes and increased use of 
emergency and hospital services.1 Empirical evidence further demonstrates the impact at the point of care: 
one recent analysis found that only a small share of requests are approved immediately, while 44% were 
approved only after a median of 6 days of PA review and 45% were ultimately denied, underscoring the 
frequency of treatment delays and barriers to appropriate therapy.2 Together, these findings highlight how PA 
requirements can disrupt care delivery and delay access to medically necessary pharmaceuticals. 
 
STS strongly supports policies that reduce barriers to timely, evidence-based care, including access to 
appropriate pharmaceuticals. We encourage CMS to ensure these API enhancements are implemented in a 
way that is user-friendly and does not inadvertently add complexity for providers. 
 
Proposed Requirement to Include a Specific Reason for Denial in Response to Prior Authorization  
Requests for All Drugs 
 
In the 2024 Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Final Rule, CMS finalized a 
requirement that, beginning in 2026, impacted payers must provide a specific reason for denial in their 
response to a provider's PA request for nondrug items and services, regardless of the method used to 
communicate the PA request or decision. CMS proposes the same requirements for denied PAs for all drugs for 
impacted payers that are not already subject to such a requirement. 
 
STS supports this proposal. Requiring clear, specific denial rationales is an important step toward improving 
transparency and addressing persistent barriers to accessing medically necessary drugs under PA. PA continues 
to create administrative burden for clinicians and delays initiation of therapy, which can contribute to 
treatment disruption and nonadherence. Standardized, actionable denial explanations are essential to 
improving the efficiency and fairness of the review process. 
 
Proposed Requirement to Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics for Drugs for Impacted Payers 
 
To incorporate drugs into the existing PA metrics, CMS proposes to require impacted payers to annually report 
certain metrics about PAs for all drugs (excluding covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs) by posting this information 
on their public website. Specifically, CMS proposes that impacted payers, other than Medicaid managed care 
plans and CHIP managed care entities, be required to annually report the previous calendar year's metrics 
regarding all drugs, excluding covered Part D drugs for MA-PDs, on their public websites beginning in 2028 
following any calendar year that any of these impacted payers offered that type of plan. 
 
1 https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/prior-authorization/prior-authorization-delays-care-and-increases-
health-care?utm_source=chatgpt.com 
2 Wang Y, Levy JF, Mattingly TJ, Anderson G. Prior Authorization and Associated Delays and Denials of Branded Medication 
Dispensation. JAMA Health Forum. 2026;7(4):e260760. doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2026.0760 
 
 
 
 
 
Expanding transparency to include non-Part D drugs is an important step toward better understanding how 
STS supports the expansion of PA transparency to include non-Part D drugs. Public reporting of key metrics—
such as approval rates, denial rates, and timeliness—will provide important insight into how utilization 
management practices affect access to medically necessary therapies and will help identify variation across 
payers. 
 
STS strongly encourages CMS to ensure that these metrics are standardized across payers to allow meaningful 
comparison. In addition, CMS should consider requiring more granular stratification where feasible, such as by 
drug class or clinical indication, to better capture access issues relevant to complex specialty care. Greater 
transparency in PA for drugs will help inform future policy efforts aimed at reducing unnecessary delays and 
ensuring timely patient access to appropriate therapies. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments. Please contact Molly Peltzman, Associate Director 
of Health Policy, at mpeltzman@sts.org should you need additional information or clarification. 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Vinay Badhwar, MD 
President

# Comment Analysis: CMS-2026-1255-0001

---

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) - Vinay Badhwar, MD, President
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Not-for-profit organization representing more than 8,000 surgeons, researchers, and allied health care professionals worldwide dedicated to heart, lung, and esophagus surgery outcomes

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

STS supports CMS's proposal to expand Prior Authorization APIs to include drugs covered under medical benefit, require specific denial reasons, and publicly report PA metrics for drugs. The organization emphasizes that PA delays significantly impede patient care and advocates for user-friendly implementation, standardized metrics, and granular stratification by drug class or clinical indication.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL, PA-DENIAL-REASONS, API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 2024 Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Final Rule
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization APIs, public website reporting

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prior Authorization APIs for Medical Benefit Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Improving accessibility and transparency of PA requirements reduces administrative burden and mitigates delays in patient access. National survey data show nearly 90% of physicians report PA delays access to necessary treatment, with many linking delays to worsening clinical outcomes and increased emergency/hospital service use. Analysis found only small share of requests approved immediately, with 44% approved after median 6 days and 45% ultimately denied.
- **Specific request:** Ensure API enhancements are user-friendly and do not inadvertently add complexity for providers.

**Topic 2: Specific Denial Reasons for Drug PA**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Clear, specific denial rationales improve transparency and address barriers to accessing medically necessary drugs. PA creates administrative burden and delays therapy initiation, contributing to treatment disruption and nonadherence. Standardized, actionable denial explanations are essential for efficiency and fairness.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirement for specific denial reasons for all drugs.

**Topic 3: Public Reporting of PA Metrics for Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with enhancement
- **Rationale:** Public reporting of approval rates, denial rates, and timeliness provides insight into how utilization management affects access to medically necessary therapies and helps identify variation across payers.
- **Specific request:** (1) Ensure metrics are standardized across payers to allow meaningful comparison; (2) Require more granular stratification where feasible, such as by drug class or clinical indication, to better capture access issues relevant to complex specialty care.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

The comment does not explicitly reference numbered solicitations but addresses topics covered by:

**Implicit responses:**
- **S12 (technical challenges for medical benefit drug PA APIs):** Emphasizes need for user-friendly implementation that does not add provider complexity
- **S16 (what is "specific reason" for denials):** Supports standardized, actionable denial explanations
- **S29 (which API usage metrics to collect):** Recommends standardized metrics including approval rates, denial rates, timeliness, with granular stratification by drug class/clinical indication
- **S35 (publish aggregate metrics):** Supports public reporting to identify variation across payers

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Ensure PA API enhancements are user-friendly and do not add provider complexity
2. Finalize requirement for specific denial reasons for all drug PA requests
3. Standardize PA metrics across all payers to enable meaningful comparison
4. Require granular stratification of metrics by drug class or clinical indication where feasible
5. Use public transparency to inform future policy efforts aimed at reducing unnecessary delays

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:**
  - PA delays impede timely patient care
  - Risk that API enhancements could inadvertently add complexity for providers
  - Need for standardization to enable meaningful cross-payer comparison
  - Current lack of granular data on access issues for complex specialty care

- **Potential negative impacts cited:**
  - Treatment delays and barriers to appropriate therapy
  - Worsening clinical outcomes
  - Increased emergency and hospital service use
  - Treatment disruption and nonadherence
  - Administrative burden on clinicians

- **Implementation barriers mentioned:**
  - Risk of adding provider complexity if not implemented carefully
  - Need for standardization across payers

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:**
  - Nearly 90% of physicians report PA delays access to necessary treatment (AMA survey data)
  - 44% of PA requests approved only after median of 6 days
  - 45% of PA requests ultimately denied
  - Only small share of requests approved immediately

- **Studies or research referenced:**
  - AMA national survey data on PA delays
  - Wang Y, Levy JF, Mattingly TJ, Anderson G. "Prior Authorization and Associated Delays and Denials of Branded Medication Dispensation." JAMA Health Forum. 2026;7(4):e260760. doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2026.0760

- **Examples provided:**
  - Link between PA delays and worsening clinical outcomes
  - Link between PA delays and increased emergency/hospital service use

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:**
  - Thoracic surgeons and surgical teams
  - Patients requiring drugs for heart, lung, esophagus conditions
  - Healthcare providers managing complex surgical care
  - Payers (MA, Medicaid, CHIP, QHPs)

- **Economic implications:**
  - PA delays increase emergency and hospital service costs
  - Administrative burden on clinicians
  - Potential cost savings from reducing unnecessary delays

- **Technical feasibility:**
  - Supports PA API approach as technically sound
  - Emphasizes importance of user-friendly implementation
  - Notes need for standardization across payers

- **Patient care impact:**
  - HIGH: PA delays impede timely access to medically necessary drugs
  - Treatment disruption and nonadherence risks
  - Worsening clinical outcomes from delays
  - Increased emergency care utilization

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Professional, evidence-based, collaborative
- **Priority level:** Medium-High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "National survey data indicate that nearly 90% of physicians report PA delays access to necessary treatment, with many linking these delays to worsening clinical outcomes and increased use of emergency and hospital services." - Context: Establishing evidence base for PA reform urgency

2. "One recent analysis found that only a small share of requests are approved immediately, while 44% were approved only after a median of 6 days of PA review and 45% were ultimately denied, underscoring the frequency of treatment delays and barriers to appropriate therapy." - Context: Citing JAMA Health Forum study on PA delays and denials

3. "STS strongly encourages CMS to ensure that these metrics are standardized across payers to allow meaningful comparison. In addition, CMS should consider requiring more granular stratification where feasible, such as by drug class or clinical indication, to better capture access issues relevant to complex specialty care." - Context: Recommendation for enhanced metrics reporting

---

## 12. THEMES

- [X] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports October 1, 2027 compliance date; emphasizes need for timely implementation

- [X] **COST-RESOURCES** - Notes administrative burden on clinicians; cites increased emergency/hospital service costs from PA delays

- [X] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Emphasizes need for user-friendly implementation that does not add complexity; notes current administrative burden

- [X] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central theme: PA delays impede timely access to medically necessary drugs; cites treatment disruption and nonadherence

- [X] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports PA API approach; emphasizes need for user-friendly, non-complex implementation

- [X] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strongly supports specific denial reasons and public metrics reporting; advocates for standardization and granular stratification

- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed

- [ ] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Not a primary focus

- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not addressed in detail

- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not challenged

- [ ] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Implicit in call for standardization across payers

- [ ] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Not a focus

- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed

- [ ] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses need to avoid adding complexity to workflows

- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed
